data.title: Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What is idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis (IGH)?**
- Common acquired benign condition of multiple small (2–5 mm), well-defined porcelain-white guttate macules on chronically sun-exposed extensor forearms and shins; increases with age (>40 years), women noticed earlier
- Considered a sign of photoageing (UV-induced melanocyte senescence), also genetic and HLA-DQ3 association

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Round/angular white macules with sharp borders, no scaling, no inflammation, stable size, do not enlarge or coalesce; asymptomatic
- Shins and forearms (dorsal), occasionally face, trunk; never on palms/soles or mucosa

**Q3. Histopathology.**
- Basket-weave hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy with flattened rete ridges, decreased melanin and reduced number of DOPA-positive melanocytes

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Vitiligo (larger, progressive, any site), guttate morphoea/lichen sclerosus (atrophic, shiny), pityriasis versicolor (scale, KOH), post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, leucoderma punctata (after PUVA), progressive macular hypomelanosis (trunk, confluent), tuberous sclerosis confetti macules, chemical leucoderma, indeterminate leprosy (sensory)

**Q5. Treatment.**
- Reassurance and sun protection
- Options for cosmetic improvement: superficial cryotherapy (2–5 s), topical tacrolimus/pimecrolimus, topical retinoids, localised dermabrasion, fractional CO2 or excimer laser, 88% phenol spot application, 5-FU with microneedling, suction blister grafts (variable results)

**Q6. What are the proposed causes of IGH?**
- Chronic UV exposure (photoageing — focal melanocyte loss), ageing/somatic mutation of melanocytes, genetic predisposition (familial), HLA-DQ3, local trauma, autoimmunity (debated)

**Q7. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Well-demarcated white areas with amoeboid/petaloid ('cloudy sky' or 'feathery') margins and absent or reduced pigment network; no perifollicular pigmentation

**Q8. How do you differentiate IGH from guttate vitiligo by Wood's lamp?**
- IGH: off-white, less bright, no enhancement of surrounding activity; vitiligo: bright chalk-white fluorescence with sharp border; histology — vitiligo has complete absence of melanocytes

**Q9. Is IGH a marker of any systemic disease?**
- No — it is benign; indicates cumulative sun damage, so counsel sun protection; patients with many IGH lesions often have other photodamage signs (solar lentigines, actinic keratoses)

**Q10. What is the age and sex distribution and prevalence?**
- Increases with age — >80% of people over 70 have some IGH; women present earlier (cosmetic concern); fair skin with heavy sun exposure but also common in Indian skin

**Q11. Explain the 'four types' on dermoscopy (Ankad classification).**
- Amoeboid, feathery, petaloid, nebuloid (cloudy) patterns of white areas with irregular borders — help differentiate from vitiligo and guttate morphoea

**Q12. Why should guttate morphoea and LS be excluded?**
- They also produce small white macules on trunk/limbs but are slightly indurated or atrophic and shiny, with follicular plugs (LS) — need different treatment; IGH is flat, non-indurated, sun-exposed

**Q13. What are the newer procedural treatments?**
- Fractional CO2 laser, 5-FU tattooing/ microneedling, excimer laser, 88% phenol 'spot peel', non-cultured epidermal cell suspension, platelet-rich plasma with microneedling — small series, variable repigmentation

**Q14. What is leucoderma punctata?**
- Multiple small white guttate macules after PUVA or psoralen + sunlight therapy — similar to IGH; also confetti-like depigmentation after imiquimod/ chemical leucoderma

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Multiple tiny porcelain-white macules on sun-exposed shins of middle-aged — IGH

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypomelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
